Mango (Mangifera indica L.), considered the 'King of fruits', is the most important commercially grown fruit of India due to its wide range of adaptability, high nutritive value, richness in variety, delicious taste, and excellent flavour. It has great export potential.
The fruit is a rich source of vitamin A and C and is utilized raw or ripe.

Collection, hybridization and evaluation of mango germplasm and hybrids for improvement of yield and quality are carried out at IIHR. Several high yielding hybrids/varieties developed and released include Arka Anmol, Arka Neelkiran, Arka Puneet, Arka Aruna, and Arka Udaya.
The total collection in the mango Field Gene Bank (FGB) comprises 667 accessions.

The cause of spongy tissue formation in Alphonso mango was identified for the first time in the world.
Characterization of indigenous seedling mango varieties was carried out using molecular characterization.

Mango trees are affected by a number of diseases including fungal and bacterial. Fungi enter plants through natural openings such as stomata and through wounds caused by pruning, harvesting, hail, insects, other diseases, and mechanical damage.
Powdery mildew is one of the serious diseases affecting most of the mango varieties.
The hopper is a major and serious pest threat to mango trees during the flowering season. If uncontrolled, they can cause severe damage and major crop loss in cases of severe infestation.
Bacterial diseases can cause a variety of symptoms including cankers, leaf spots, overgrowths, scabs, wilts, and others.

Anthracnose is the most important disease in mango in states like Bihar, Punjab, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Kerala, UP, AP, Rajasthan, and Karnataka.

On older spots, infected tissues fall off giving a shot hole appearance.

content: Produces leaf spots, blossom blight, wither tip, twigs blight and fruit rot. Small blister like spots develop on the leaves and twigs. Young leaves wither and dry Tender twigs wither and die back symptom appears. Affected branches ultimately dry up. Black spots appear on fruits. The fruit pulp becomes hard, crack and decay at ripening. Infected fruits drop.
Spray P. fluorescens (FP 7) at 3 weeks interval commencing from October at 5g/like on flower branches. 5-7 sprays one to be given on flowers and bunches.
Before storage, treat with hot water, (50-55°C) for 15 minutes or dip in Benomyl solution (500ppm) or Thiobendazole (1000ppm) for 5 minutes.

It attacks the leaves, flowers, stalks of panicle and fruits. Shedding of infected leaves occurs when the disease is severe. The affected fruits do not grow in size and may drop before attaining pea size.
Survives as dormant mycelium in affected leaves. Secondary spread is by air borne conidia.

Dusting the plants with fine sulphur (250-300 mesh) at the rate of 0.5 kg/tree. The first application may be soon after flowering, second 15 days later (or) spray with Wettable sulphur (0.2%), (or) Carbendazim (0.1%), (or) Tridemorph (0.1%), (or) Karathane (0.1%).

Three types of symptoms occur: bunchy top phase, floral malformation, and vegetative malformation. In bunchy top phase in nursery, bunching of thickened small shoots bearing small rudimentally leaves occurs, where shoots remain short and stunted giving a bunchy top appearance. In vegetative malformation, seedlings show excessive vegetative branches of limited growth that are swollen with short internodes forming bunches of various size, with the top of seedlings showing a bunchy top appearance. In malformation of inflorescence, variation in the panicle is shown; the malformed head dries up in a black mass and persists for a long time, and secondary branches are transformed into a number of small leaves giving a witches broom appearance.
Diseased plants should be destroyed. Use disease-free planting material. Prune diseased parts along the basal 15-20 cm apparently healthy portions.
Incidence can be reduced by spraying 100-200 ppm NAA during October. Pruning should be followed by spraying of Carbendazim (0.1%) or Captafol (0.2%).

Symptoms include dark epicarp around the base of the pedicel. In the initial stage, the affected area enlarges to form a circular, black patch. Under humid atmosphere, it extends rapidly and turns the whole fruit completely black within two or three days. The pulp becomes brown and somewhat softer.
The pathogen resides in dead twigs and bark of the trees and is spread by rains.
Prune and destroy infected twigs.
Spray Carbendazim or Thiophanate Methyl (0.1%) or Chlorathalonil (0.2%) at fortnightly intervals during the rainy season.

Symptoms of Black mould rot (Aspergillus niger) include: yellowing of base with the development of irregular, hazy, greyish spots; mesocarp of the rotted area becomes depressed and soft; the fruit surface becomes covered with blackish fungal growth; and a decrease in ascorbic acid.
The affected area of fruits becomes olivaceous-black and shrinks. Black dots appear at the centre of the spots represent the acervuli.
On matured green fruits, small brown spots appear with greyish white centre which later turn to bigger lesions with large number of acervuli seen as black dots.
Symptoms include brown spot on leaves, black spots on twigs, and black spots on fruits.
Epidemiology conditions: Temperature between 20 and 250 C (likely 20 and 25°C). Mycelial growth with sporulation takes place at pH 5.5 to 6.0. Wounding leads to more disease incidence.

Algae attacks foliage and young twigs. Rusty spots appear on leaves, initially as circular, slightly elevated, coalesce to form irregular spots. The spores mature fall off and leave cream to white valvet texture on the surface of the leaves.
Bordeaux mixture (0.6%) or Copper oxychloride 0.25%
Brown spots develop on the margin and at the tip of the leaf lamina. They increase in size and become dark brown. Black dots appear on the spots which are acervuli of the fungus.
The fungus survives on mango leaves for over a year and spreads through wind borne conidia.
Heavy infection is noticed during the monsoon when the temperature is 20-25°C and high humidity.
Remove and destroy infected plant parts.
Spraying copper oxychloride 0.25, Mancozeb 0.25% or Bordeaux mixture 1.0%.

content: The fungi produce mycelium which is superficial and dark. They grow on sugary secretions of plant hoppers, jassids, aphids and scale insects. A black encrustation is formed on the leaf surface which affects photosynthetic activity.
Management should be done for insects and sooty moulds simultaneously. Control insects by spraying systemic insecticides like methyl dematon.
Spray starch solution prepared with 1 kg Starch/Maida boiled in 5 litres of water and diluted to 20 litres. The starch dries and forms flakes which are removed along with the fungus.

Infection occurs on leaves, stems, young flowers and fruit. Sunken black spots appear on the surface of the fruit during ripening. Infection on fruit is usually latent and manifests itself only as the mango begins to ripen. The disease is most severe during wet weather.

Inoculum remains on dried leaves, defoliated branches, mummified flowers and flower brackets. Spread occurs through air-borne conidia. The fungus can enter the pores of green fruits. Latent infection of mature fruits may take place through lenticels. The fungus infects the fruits when green and develops in the flesh during ripening. Latent infection is carried from the field to storage.
The optimum temperature is 250°C (stated as 250°C in text) and relative humidity is from 95 to 97 per cent.

Spray with mancozeb (800 g/kg at 2 g/L) weekly during flowering and then monthly until harvest. Stop spraying 14 days before harvest. During dry weather, flower sprays may be reduced to fortnightly intervals.
Should rain occur during flowering, apply prochloraz (462 g/kg) (Octave) using 1 g product/L in a tank mix with mancozeb. Prochloraz only needs to be applied every 3-4 weeks.

Copper oxychloride sprays (4 g/L) used for bacterial black spot control also control anthracnose; however, copper oxychloride should not be used during flowering. Where bacterial black spot is serious, copper oxychloride can be substituted for mancozeb sprays after flowering.

Hot carbendazim (Spin Flo, liquid formulation) is registered for postharvest treatment in Queensland, Northern Territory, Western Australia, and New South Wales. Dip fruit within 24 hours of harvest by totally submerging them for 5 minutes in hot water (52°C) with 100 mL product /100 L water. Lowering the temperature below 52°C reduces effectiveness. Temperature must be controlled to within 0.5°C to prevent fruit damage. Use an accurate thermometer to monitor temperatures. Use an approximate ratio of 3 litres of dip to 1 kg of fruit. This dip also partially controls stem end rot.

Use vigorous agitation before and during dipping via a powerful recirculating pump to keep fungicide suspended and distribute heat. Bleed sap from fruit before dipping, as mango sap affects suspension stability. Prewashing fruit helps prolong dip life. Replace dip once contaminated by sap and dirt, or after 3 days continuous use, or after 4000 trays have been treated. Dipping temperatures should not exceed 52°C to prevent skin damage. Allow fruit to cool before brushing. During wet weather, reduce dipping temperature to 50°C as susceptibility to skin damage increases (disease control will be reduced at this lower temperature).

Unheated prochloraz (Sportak) spray can be used as an alternative to hot carbendazim dip. Apply prochloraz 45% at 55 mL/100 L of water at ambient temperature as a non-recirculated spray over fruit, ensuring complete coverage. Prochloraz is not effective against stem end rot. Note that postharvest treatments will not provide complete disease control.

In fruits, the pericarp darkens near the base of the pedicel. The affected area enlarges to form a circular, black patch which under humid atmosphere extends rapidly and turns the whole fruit completely black within two or three days. The pulp becomes brown and softer.
Avoid harvesting immature fruit.

Postharvest treatment with hot water and carbendazim (Spin Flo) is partially effective against stem end rot. For control of stem end rot during controlled atmosphere storage, a dual treatment of hot carbendazim (Spin Flo) followed by prochloraz is necessary.

Fruit from orchards with a history of stem end rot losses should be rejected for long term storage. The severity of stem end rot can be assessed by harvesting 100 mature fruit at random from throughout the orchard, leaving them untreated and storing at 25° until they are fully ripe. Ideally, less than one-tenth and certainly no more than one-third of the fruit should develop symptoms of stem end rot by the time they are fully ripe.

Epicarp darkens around the base - pedicel. Circular, black patch develops under humid atmosphere. Soft rot develops with the aid of pectinolytic & cellulolytic enzymes. More portions of fruit turn black and soften. The fruit loses ascorbic acid & non-reducing sugars rapidly.
The fungus persists in infected plant parts which serve as source of inoculum.
Favorable epidemiological conditions include relative humidity (RH) of 80%, with maximum and minimum temperatures of 31.5°C and 25.90°C.
Symptoms include discrete and discoloured areas all over that turn dark brown – black at maturity. Black fruit in bodies appear on the spots.
The disease is soil-borne. Conidia are transmitted by wind and rain water.

Symptoms can be noticed on the inflorescence, stalk of inflorescence, leaves, and young fruits. The characteristic symptoms are white superficial powdery growth of the fungus on these parts. Infected flowers may fall prematurely and young fruits may remain on the tree until they reach marble size and then drop prematurely.
Dropping of unfertilized infected flowers and young fruits leads to serious crop loss (20-80%).
Conidia development occurs at 9-32 °C & >25% R.H. Disease development occurs at 10-31 °C & 60-90% R.H. The disease is associated with phosphorus deficiency.
Pruning of diseased leaves and malformed panicles reduces primary inoculums.
Three sprays of systemic fungicides during flowering season are recommended at 12-15 days intervals. The 1st spray is recommended when there is 25% flower opening.

Anthracnose manifests on different parts of the mango tree. On the inflorescence, the earliest symptoms are the production of blackish brown specks on peduncles and flowers. Small black spots appear on the panicles and open flowers, which gradually enlarge and cause death of flowers. The infected flowers fall off, leaving persistent spikes on the peduncles.
Infection and dropping of flowers leads to serious crop loss (10-90%).
Favorable environmental conditions are 25-30 °C & 95-97% R.H. The disease is associated with excessive nitrogen.
Diseased leaves, flowers, twigs and fruits lying on the floor of the orchard should be collected and all infected twigs from the tree should be pruned and burnt.
Blossom infection can be controlled effectively by two to three sprays of contact or systemic fungicides during spring season at 12-15 days interval.
Malformation is a serious threat to the mango growing areas of Pakistan as it causes crop loss up to 70%. Recent findings have demonstrated that the disease may be of fungal origin.

Vegetative malformation is more pronounced in young seedlings as well as seedling trees than in grafted plants. Affected seedlings develop excessive vegetative branches, which are of limited growth, swollen, and have very short internodes.
Malformation of inflorescence (MF) is a disease of inflorescence. The most characteristic symptoms are the reduction and compactness of internodes, giving the malformation a broom-like appearance.
Infected grafting material and wounds contribute to the spread and occurrence of the disease.

At present, no definite control measures can be advocated. However, incidence can be reduced by: avoiding scion sticks from trees bearing malformed inflorescence for propagation; using only certified saplings for propagation; and pruning affected terminals along with the contiguous 15-20cm apparently healthy portion and burning them as soon as disease symptoms are well expressed.
Mango plants are prone to various leaf diseases, with the most important ones being Anthracnose, Scab, and Phoma blight.
Characteristics symptoms appear as oval or irregular brown to deep brown spot of various sizes scattered all over the leaf surface. Young leaves are more prone to attack than the older ones.
Under damp conditions, the fungus grows rapidly. Insect attack may facilitate the entry of pathogen resulting into heavy incidence of disease.
The foliar infection can be controlled by sprays of copper based fungicides during spring and after monsoon season.

Symptoms first appear as small, brownish circular spots on the surface of leaves. Later on, high concentration of brown black spots occurs evenly over the leaf lamina. Symptoms are more prominent on the lower side of the leaves. The tender leaves are found to be more susceptible than mature ones.
The disease can be controlled by regular field spray program including copper based fungicides.

On leaves, minute water soaked irregular to angular raised lesions is usually crowded at the apex. On young leaves halos are larger and distinct, while on older leaves, they are narrow could be observed only against light. Under severe infections, the leaf turns yellow and drop off.
Bacterial canker development is associated with 25-30 °C, >90% R.H., and rainy weather.
Control includes regular inspection of orchards and sanitation.
Seedling certification is recommended as a preventive measure against the disease.
Spray of copper based fungicides has been found effective in controlling bacterial canker.

The disease is more common on young fruits and during transit and storage. Latent infection during pre-harvest stage is responsible for post harvest rots. On storage, black spots are produced, initially round but later forming large irregular blotches on the entire fruits. The spots have large deep cracks and the fungus penetrates deep into the fruit causing extensive rotting.

Pre-harvest infections can be managed by spraying copper based fungicides after completion of heavy showers. Post harvest infections can be managed via pre-harvest sprays in the field to reduce latent infection, and treatment of the fruit with hot water/fungicides after harvest to eradicate left over latent infection.

Research on Ataulfo mangos in Nayarit, Chiapas, and Guerrero focuses on modifying parthenocarpic fruit production, assessing inflorescence development, floral biology (pollination, fertilization, and fruit set), and validating techniques to increase fruit set and size of parthenocarpic fruit.
Mango (Mangifera indica L.) is one of the oldest and most popular fruits having delightful flavour and taste of the tropical world.

India leads the world in mango production, accounting for 65 per cent of global production. Currently, mango is cultivated in India across an area of 2.3 million hectares with a total production of 12.75 million tonnes.

Average mango productivity in India is 5.5 metric tonnes per hectare, which is low compared to 35-40 metric tonnes per hectare realized in Israel. Productivity in India declined from 8.1 t/ha in 1991-92 to 5.5 t/ha in 2008-09.

Despite contributing 65 per cent to global production, India's share in the world fresh mango market is only 5.25 per cent in terms of quantity and 3.5 per cent in terms of value. Importing countries consider India a source of quality mangoes due to its varietal wealth and availability.

Mango belongs to the family Anacardiaceae.

Popular varieties in mango include Neelum, Bangalora, Alphonso, Rumani, Banganapalli, Kalepad, Peter, PKM 1, PKM 2, Sendura, Jahangir, Mulgoa, Himayuddin, Paiyur 1, Mallika, Amrapali, Salem Bangalora, Arka Anmol, Arka Aruna, Arka Neelkiran, Arka Puneeth, and Sindhu.
Varieties suitable for Tamil Nadu are Banganapalli, Bangalora, Neelum, Rumani, Mulgoa, Alphonso, Senthura, Kalepad, and Imam Pasand.
Processing varieties include Alphonso, Banganapalli, and Totapuri. Export varieties include Alphonso, Banganapalli, and Sendura.
Ideal soil for mango is red loamy. Good drainage is preferable for better establishment. The ideal pH range is from 6.5 to 8.0.
Planting season spreads from July to December.
Approach and epicotyl grafts are used for planting.
Dig pits of 1 m x 1 m x 1 m. Fill in with topsoil mixed with 10 kg of FYM and 100 g per pit.

Under conventional planting systems, adopt a spacing of 7-10 m either way. Under High Density Planting (HDP), adopt 5 m x 5 m (400 plants/ha). Under the double hedge row system, adopt a spacing of 5 m x 5 m within double rows and 10 m between successive double rows (266 plants/ha).
Grafts are planted in the centre of the pit with the ball of earth intact, followed by watering and staking. The graft union must be 15 cm above the ground level.

Regular watering is recommended till establishment. Under conventional irrigation systems, weekly irrigation is essential. Under micro-irrigation, water requirement is restricted to one-third of the conventional method.
Short duration crops like legumes, vegetables, and groundnut can be raised as intercrops during the pre-bearing age.

Apply manures and fertilizers per tree as follows: In the 1st year, apply 10.00 kg FYM, 0.20 kg N, 0.20 kg P, and 0.30 kg K. Increase annually by 10.00 kg FYM, 0.20 kg N, 0.20 kg P, and 0.30 kg K. From the 6th year onwards, apply 50 kg FYM, 1.0 kg N, 1.0 kg P, and 1.5 kg K. Apply in September–October, 45 to 90 cm away from the trunk up to the peripheral leaf drip, and incorporate.

Under HDP, apply 1.0:0.5:1.0 kg NPK per bearing tree per year through drip fertigation: Immediately after harvest (2 months) apply 25% N, 50% P, 25% K; Pre-flowering (2 months) apply 40% N, 30% P, 20% K; Flowering to fruit set (2 months) apply 20% N, 20% P, 25% K; Fruit development (4 months) apply 15% N, 0% P, 30% K. At each stage, split into six or more doses and apply at weekly intervals. Avoid irrigation and fertigation for 30 days before flowering to induce stress; resume when flowering commences.

Remove root stock sprouts and low-lying branches. In old trees, remove overlapping, intercrossing, diseased, dried, and weak branches. Carry out judicious pruning of internal branches during August–September once every three years. Prevent flowering up to three years by removing inflorescences as they appear. Retain two healthy shoots by trimming weak shoots among crowded terminal shoots during August–September annually. Prune back 20 cm of annual growth of terminals immediately after harvest.

For top working senile orchards, use scions of choice varieties like Alphonso and Banganapalli. Behead trees during July–August leaving the main trunk at a convenient height to develop new shoots. Perform cleft grafting or softwood grafting on emerging shoots on the main stem during September–October.

Spray NAA @ 20 ppm at flowering to increase fruit retention. During February, spray 0.5% Urea (5 g/lit) or 1% Potassium Nitrate (10 g/lit) to induce flowering if trees fail to flower. Spray 2% KNO3 at mustard size to increase fruit set and retention. Apply Paclobutrazol @ 10 g a.i. for non-bearing trees during the first fortnight of September to induce flowering and fruit set yield during off years.

Spray two rounds of acephate 75 SP @ 1 g/lit, phosalone 35 EC @ 1.5 ml/lit, carbaryl 50 WP @ 2 g/lit, or phosphamidon 40 SL @ 2 ml/lit of water: first at panicle emergence and second two weeks later. Spray wettable sulphur @ 2 g/lit after carbaryl to avoid mite resurgence. Phosphamidon + neem oil 5 ml/lit can be mixed with insecticides to control hopper and shoot webber.
Application of Dimethoate or Methyl demeton @ 2 ml/lit controls leaf galls and aphids.
Application of Phosalone 35 EC @ 2 ml/lit controls flower webber.
Spray Fenthion 100 EC @ 1 ml/lit during the marble stage, followed by a second spray 15 days after the first spray to control nut weevil.

Spray Chlorpyriphos 20 EC @ 2.5 ml/lit or Monocrotophos 36 WSC @ 1.5 ml/lit. Band the tree trunks with 20 cm wide 400-gauge polythene sheets to prevent pest ascent. Release the Australian ladybird beetle, Cryptolaemus montrouzieri, @ 10 per tree as a biocontrol measure.

Soak absorbent cotton in 10 ml Monocrotophos (36 WSC) and place it on the affected stem by removing 2.5 cm² of bark, then wrap with gunny or plastic sheet (do not treat during the bearing stage). Alternatively, mechanically remove or kill the grub with a needle or wire, apply carbofuran 3 G @ 5 g per bore hole, and plug with mud.

Spray Fenthion @ 2 ml/lit or Malathion @ 2 ml/lit. Plough inter-spaces to expose pupae. Install pheromone traps containing 1 ml methyl eugenol + 1 ml malathion solution in 1 litre water (use 10 ml mixture per trap placed in 25 locations/ha between 6 a.m. and 8 a.m.) to trap and kill insects. Collect and destroy fallen fruits.
Dust Sulphur (350 mesh) in the early morning to protect new flush, or spray Wettable sulphur 0.2% or Tridemorph 0.05% to control powdery mildew.
Pre-harvest spraying of Mancozeb @ 2 g/lit, Carbendazim @ 1 g/lit, Thiophanate methyl @ 1 g/lit, or Chlorothalonil @ 2 g/lit three times at 15-day intervals controls anthracnose and stalk end-rot.
Spray Phosphamidon 40 SL @ 2 ml/litre + Maida 5% (1 kg Maida or starch boiled with 1 lit of water and diluted to 20 litres) to control sooty mould. Avoid spraying during cloudy weather.

Use disease-free planting material and destroy diseased plants. Reduce incidence by spraying 100-200 ppm NAA during October. Prune diseased parts including the basal 15-20 cm of apparently healthy portions, followed by spraying Carbendazim (0.1%).

Harvest mangoes on a clear dry day and avoid injury during all handling stages. In the field, spray Carbendazim (0.1%) or Chlorothalonil (0.2%). Post-harvest, dip mangoes in 6% borax solution at 43°C for 3 minutes.
Spray Bordeaux mixture (1%) or Copper oxychloride 0.25% to control red rust.
Harvest spreads from March to June. Yield varies with varieties and spacing: 8 to 10 t/ha up to 15 years, and 15 to 20 t/ha from 15 to 20 years.

Dip fruits in hot water at 52 ± 1°C immediately after harvest for 5 minutes followed by application of 8% plant wax (Fruitox or Waxol) to reduce anthracnose disease during storage. Two pre-harvest sprays of 0.20% Mancozeb (2.0 g/lit) also reduce disease incidence.
Waiting periods between application and harvest: Dimethoate: 14 days; Methyl demeton 0.05%: 14 days; Fenthion 0.05%: 14 days; Quinalphos 0.05%: 12 days.

Growing districts: Krishnagiri, Vellore, Dindigul, Thiruvallur, Dharmapuri, Theni. Major Tamil Nadu markets: Theni, Dharmapuri, Salem, Tirunelveli. Preferred varieties: Banganapalli, Bangalora, Neelum, Rumani, Mulgoa, Alphonso, Totapuri. Export markets: UAE, Kuwait, and other Middle East countries. Grade specifications require firmness, lack of decay/defects, uniformity of size/shape, skin/flesh color, and flavor. Weight grades: Small (<200 g), Medium (201-400 g), Large (401-600 g), Extra-large (601-800 g).
Collection and destruction of fallen fruits will prevent the multiplication of stone weevil and fruit fly.
Deep ploughing around tree trunk during summer months helps in killing the eggs of mealy bugs and matured larvae and pupae of fruit fly.
Removal of weed plants like Bhattar Clerodendron infortunatum and other grasses will check the buildup of population of mealy bug.

Banding the tree trunk with 20 cm wide alkathene (400 guage) and applying grease on it in the 2nd week of Dec, before mealy bug starts ascending, is effective in arresting the climbing of crawlers of mealy bugs.

pest: leaf webber, shoot borer, shoot gall psyllid
content: The infestation of leaf webber, shoot borer, shoot gall psyllid can be controlled by 2 -3 application of fenvelerate (0.01%), permethrin (0.02%) and dimethoate (0.06%) at 21 days interval commencing from Aug.
Injection of petrol, kerosene emulsion of dichlorovos or EDCT mixture in the tunnel after cleaning and sealing it with mud has been recommended for break and stem borer of mango.
No bio control agent has been found effective on a large scale.

Although India is the largest mango producer in the world, productivity is considerably low. One of the major reasons is the occurrence of diseases causing huge losses every year at both pre- and post-harvest stages, limiting profitability to growers.

Diverse climatic conditions in India predispose mango to the incidence of over 140 pathogens causing damages of varying intensities at different production stages, alongside several physiological disorders that also affect production.

Effective disease management schedules integrate cultural, mechanical, biological, and chemical strategies. Because diseases are sensitive at their critical periods, management interventions and need-based cultural operations should be timed at the most optimum periods for efficient control.

Mango (Mangifera indica L.) is considered the king of all fruits, known for its delicious taste, excellent flavour, and high content of vitamins A and C. In India, it is cultivated across an area of 1.23 million hectares with a production of 10.99 million tonnes.

Mango production faces severe constraints from various insect pests and diseases from the seedling to the maturity stage. Excessive chemical pesticide applications lead to environmental pollution, ecological imbalance, pesticide resistance, pest resurgence, and harmful residues in produce; Integrated Pest Management (IPM) strategies should be adopted with chemical pesticides reserved as a last resort.

scientific_name: Orthaga euadrusalis Walker and O. exvinacea Hampson
content: Leaf webbers are medium-sized and sombre-coloured. Neonate larvae scrape chlorophyll from leaves, while second instar larvae (8-10 in number) web leaves and shoots together, feeding until only midribs and veins remain. Infested clusters of leaves turn dry and brown and can be spotted from a distance.

growth_stage: tender shoots, flowering, and marble-sized fruit stage
content: Adults and late instar nymphs are flat, oval-shaped, and covered with waxy whitish powder; they colonize tree trunk bark. Adult females and nymphs feed on tender shoots, flowers, and marble-sized fruits, causing shrivelling, drying of young shoots and panicles, reduced fruit size, and premature fruit dropping. They also excrete honeydew which promotes sooty mould development.

growth_stage: vegetative, flowering, and mature fruit stage
content: Thrips are tiny, pale yellow or whitish insects with dark body setae and fringe wings. They colonize and feed on fresh leaves, inflorescences, and fruits by lacerating tissues, resulting in wilting, drying, reduced fruit set, and bronzing of mature fruits.

Adults are long, stout, dark beetles measuring 50-60 mm in length. Neonate grubs feed peripherally beneath the bark, while larvae bore deep into the sapwood creating 2-3 cm wide tunnels. Symptoms include sticky fluid oozing from trees, frass exuding from trunk bore holes, branch yellowing, drying, and dieback of terminal shoots, ultimately causing tree death.

Adult flies emerge in April and puncture the skin of mature fruits to deposit clusters of 6-15 banana-shaped eggs 1-4 mm deep into the mesocarp. Infested fruits exhibit small ovipositional marks with oozing fluid, rot prematurely, and turn unfit for consumption due to large numbers of developing larvae inside.

growth_stage: vegetative, flowering, and immature fruit stage
scientific_name: Idioscopus clypealis, I. nitidulus and Amritodus atkinsoni
content: Hoppers possess a wedge-shaped body, broad head, narrow posterior abdomen, and hind legs modified for quick hopping. Both nymphs and adults suck sap from tender shoots, inflorescences, and leaves, causing poor flower set, premature fruit drop, and yield reduction. Excreted honeydew fosters the development of sooty mould.

Symptoms consist of white superficial powdery fungal growth on leaves, panicle stalks, flowers, and young fruits. The disease hampers fruit set, induces fruit drop, and can cause yield losses of up to 90 percent.

growth_stage: flowering, young fruit, mature fruit, and post-harvest storage
content: A major pre- and post-harvest disease that affects leaves, twigs, flowers, young fruits, and mature fruits in storage. Manifests as slightly black, sunken, irregular lesions that gradually expand.

Characterized by twigs drying downwards from the top (especially in older trees), followed by leaf drying that gives a fire-scorched appearance. Internal wood tissues show browning when split along the longitudinal axis, and branches develop cracks and exude gum before dying.
Avoid dense planting, prune overcrowded and overlapping branches. Plough regularly and remove the weeds from orchard.
Install yellow and blue sticky traps (50/ha) for hopper and thrips management.

Apply entomopathogens like Metarhizium anisopliae and Beauveria bassiana and botanicals viz., azadirachtin 1% @ 3 ml/l, lemon grass oil (0.125%) and citronella oil (0.25%), when the hopper population is low (<4/panicle).
Apply need based label claim insecticides viz., imidacloprid 17.8 SL (0.03%) or thiamethoxam 25 WG (0.05%) for hopper and thrips management.
Remove leaf webs periodically and destroy for leaf webber management.
Flood irrigation of orchard during October kill eggs of mealy bug.
Plough the orchard during November-December to expose different stages of mealy bugs to natural enemies. Remove nearby alternate weed host, Clerodendrum infortunatum to reduce infestation.
Banding tree trunk with alkathene sheet (400 guage) 30 cm above ground level with 25 cm wide and apply grease from lower end of alkathene which prevents infestation from crawling nymphs.
Apply biopesticides like Beauveria bassiana (0.4%) or 5% NSKE around tree trunk during second week of December.
Spray Dimethoate 30 EC (0.06%) to manage the nymphs of mealy bugs ascending on the tree.
Prune infested branches and remove dead trees infested with stem borer. Install light traps during May-June to catch adult borers.
Remove grubs using wire or hook from the holes of infested tree trunks and kill. Insert aluminum phosphide tablets or cotton dipped in petrol and plug with mud plaster.
Apply IIHR, Bengaluru formulation “Arka borer control” on stem from base upto 2.5-3 feet to prevent egg laying by stem borer (www.iihr.res.in).
Plough orchard in the month of November – December to expose fruit fly pupae to sunlight and predators.
Collect and destroy infested fallen fruits in regular intervals to reduce fruit fly population.
Install methyl eugenol traps from reliable source @ 6/acre during fruiting period from April- August.
Apply bait splashes on tree trunk and branches with 10% jaggery + deltamethrin (0.1%) to attract and kill female fruit flies.
Immerse mango fruits in hot water at 48°C for 60 min. within 24 hrs of harvest to kill the eggs without altering quality.

Prune plants to facilitate periodically spraying with spray equipment and improve air circulation in the canopy. Pick up fallen mango foliage and destroy it. Periodically remove severely infected panicles. Intercrop mango with other compatible fruit trees or forestry species. Keep mango trees weed free to manage powdery mildew.

growth_stage: before flowering and immediately after fruit formation
content: Before flowering and immediately after fruit formation spray need based label claim fungicides, viz., sulphur 80 WP @ 0.3% or hexaconazole 5EC @ 0.1% to manage powdery mildew.
Remove malformed flowers & paste the cut portion with Bordeaux mixture. Resort 1% Bordeux mixture or carbendezim 50 WP @ 0.1% or thiophanate 70 WP @ 0.2% to manage mango anthracnose.
Prune the infected branches and remove dead trees from the orchard. Apply Blitox 50 WP @ 0.2% for mango dieback management.
Conserve natural predators like coccinellids, predatory thrips, predatory mites, anthocorid bugs, minute pirate bugs, ground beetles, lacewings, hoverflies and spiders for hopper and thrips control.

Out of the total harvest, almost 15-20% of mango fruits spoil, with postharvest losses ranging from 0 to 80% depending on factors and practices. Fungi are the most common cause of mango fruit decay after harvest, which can be decreased through effective pre- and post-harvest practices.

Mango fruits are relatively resistant to infection during early stages of growth, but vulnerability rises as they mature. Fruits become very sensitive between harvest and consumption due to biochemical changes. Fruit rotting is caused by both saprophytic and pathogenic fungi.

Anthracnose is caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, which infects every tender part of the mango tree, including developing and mature fruits. It is the most serious postharvest disease globally, particularly in areas with frequent rains during fruit development and maturity.

Favourable conditions for infection include optimum temperature of 20-30°C, high relative humidity, prolonged rainfall, or heavy dew. Conidial germination requires free water on the fruit surface and high humidity for over 10 hours. If storage temperatures rise to 40°C during ripening, severe rotting is more likely.

Infection can remain quiescent and symptomless during fruit development, with decay and rotting appearing after harvest during ripening. Symptoms appear as dark lesions on harvested fruits. The infection initially stays in the epicarp before quickly spreading to the pulp, causing the entire fruit to rot within a few days in severe cases.

scientific_name: Lasiodiplodia theobromae, Aspergillus niger, Phomopsis mangiferae, Dithiorella dominicana, Colletotrichum gloeosporioides
content: Stem-end rot is the second most economically important postharvest disease of mango fruits. It is caused by several fungi, including Lasiodiplodia theobromae, Aspergillus niger, Phomopsis mangiferae or Dithiorella dominicana, and Colletotrichum gloeosporioides.

The fungi causing stem-end rot can be found in soil and fallen leaves, from which fruit can become infected post-harvest. The pathogen enters mango trees via natural openings or wounds and causes latent infection entering through the stem ends. Under high humidity, conidia are dispersed and released with free water. The pathogen survives the winter on trees or in the soil.
Stem-end rot is more common in orchards with older trees, in regions with high rainfall, and when fruits are stored for extended periods.

The fungi remain latently infected within branches and twigs. Endophytic hyphae colonize the inflorescence and extend to the stem end several weeks after flowering, remaining dormant in unripe fruit until harvest. During ripening, fruit rots near the stem end, turning brown-grey and soft, eventually rotting the entire fruit surface. Physical contact between healthy and decaying fruits spreads the infection.
P. mangiferae causes firmer, more defined lesions that spread more slowly than lesions caused by other stem-end rot fungi.

The disease begins as light-coloured water-soaked spots that progress into dark star-shaped cankers. Bacterial infection is confirmed by the oozing of a gummy substance from cracks caused by infection. Severely infected fruits may rot when exposed to high humidity during storage, and saprophytic fungi can colonize the damaged tissue.

scientific_name: Aspergillus spp. (A. niger, A. variecolor, A. nidulans, A. fumigatus, A. flavus, A. chevalieri)
content: The fungus enters fruit through wounds or cut ends after harvest. Infection begins as pale brown, soft, sunken spots that coalesce into rapidly spreading dark brown to black lesions, which later develop heavy fungal growth. The disease progresses more quickly at 30-36°C.

scientific_name: Botryosphaeria ribis, Ceratocystis paradoxa, Pestalotiopsis versicolor, Macrophomina phaseolina, M. mangiferae, Alternaria tenuissima, Phoma mangiferae, Rhizopus arrhizus, Cladosporium herbarum, Cladosporium cladosporioides, Fusarium oxysporum, Rhizoctonia solani
content: Postharvest fruit rotting can be caused by infection or infestation by Botryosphaeria ribis, Ceratocystis paradoxa, Pestalotiopsis versicolor, Macrophomina phaseolina, M. mangiferae, Alternaria tenuissima, Phoma mangiferae, Rhizopus arrhizus, Cladosporium herbarum, Cladosporium cladosporioides, Fusarium oxysporum, and Rhizoctonia solani.

Canopy that allows free flow of air and light penetration creates a microclimate resistant to most diseases. Rain facilitates pathogen invasion and inoculum development. During the monsoon season, temperatures drop to ideal levels for fungi to infect mature fruits, staying dormant until ripening triggers severe rotting.
Ploughing, weed management, pruning of infected twigs, and removal of fallen leaves, twigs, and fruits help reduce pathogen inoculum build-up and minimize disease incidence.

disease: sooty mould, shoulder browning, sooty blotch
content: In orchards where integrated pest management practices are used throughout the year, harvested fruits are safe. Controlling sucking pests makes sooty moulds less likely to develop, resulting in reduced incidence of shoulder browning and sooty blotch.

Fruits should be harvested when fully mature and without injury to avoid infection, infestation, and rotting. The best option is picking fruits with a 2 cm stalk portion by hand with secateurs, keeping them gently in plastic crates, de-sapping, hot water treatment, cooling, drying, and packing into CF Boxes.
New orchards should not be planted in areas that receive a lot of rain during the fruiting season to help manage postharvest diseases.
Taking care of each new flush and maintaining orchard sanitation can help reduce anthracnose fungus inoculum build-up within the canopy.
Pruning and orchard sanitation can reduce latent infection of the stem end rot pathogen in branches and twigs.
Covering fruits with paper bags is effective for postharvest disease management.

Pre-harvest sprays of fungicides (difenoconazole 25EC @ 0.05%, propineb 70WP @ 0.2%, thiophanate methyl 70WP @ 0.1%, azoxystrobin 23SC @ 0.1%) performed 21-30 days before harvest resulted in excellent disease control.
Bacillus licheniformis, Bacillus pumilus, and Bacillus subtilis have been found to be effective against anthracnose when applied to fruits after harvest.
Hot water treatment of fruits at 52±1 °C for 10 minutes is a safe, convenient, and effective method for controlling all pathogens that cause postharvest rots.
Castor oil, eucalyptus oil, lemongrass oil, and extracts of garlic bulb, Azadirachta indica, Zingiber officinale, Lantana, and Curcuma longa are effective against anthracnose.
Dashehari has the highest risk of black tip disorder, while Lucknow Safeda has the lowest.

Fruits are affected at the marble stage, showing distinctive yellowing of tissues at the distal end. The colour fades into brown and finally black. Fruit development is slowed, and the black spot extends towards the upper part of the fruit. Affected fruits ripen prematurely and yield very low returns.

Black tip has a greater impact on orchards located near brick kilns due to brick kiln fumes. There is an inverse relationship between disorder incidence and the distance of the orchard from the brick kiln.

Spraying borax or washing soda on fruits at the marble stage is effective in controlling black tip. Borax undergoes alkaline hydrolysis in water and acts as a buffering agent against acidic constituents of brick kiln fumes. Other alkaline compounds, such as caustic soda and washing soda, are also beneficial.

growth_stage: initial stages / prior to physiological maturity
content: During the initial stages of internal necrosis, water-soaked brownish areas develop on fruits and coalesce to form dark brown patches on the internal surface. The lower part of the affected fruit turns brown, sometimes black with corky and leathery skin. Affected fruits drop off before attaining physiological maturity.
Internal necrosis can be corrected by soil application of boron @ 250 g per tree incorporated at the time of October fertilization.
A foliar spray of 1% borax is recommended when fruits attain pea size, followed by two more sprays at 10-15 days intervals to minimise internal necrosis.
Cracked fruits deteriorate quickly, frequently suffer secondary infestation by disease and pest, and eventually become unmarketable, causing significant financial loss.
Pre-harvest sprays of NAA, potassium, and boron, along with maintaining adequate soil moisture during the dry period, are beneficial in reducing fruit cracking.

Fruit drop is very high at the early stages of development and continues at a low rate until fruits reach more than half size. Initial set varies from 23.5 to 74.5 fruits per panicle, but harvest retention is only 0.4 to 0.8 fruits per panicle. The primary factor for early fruit drop is a low level of auxins and gibberellins combined with a high level of ABA and ethylene.

Fruit drop can be significantly reduced by mulching and irrigation during fruit development, application of plant growth regulator NAA at 20 ppm, timely and effective control measures against major pests and diseases, and providing proper nutrition.

Clustering or 'Jhumka' is characterized by the formation of a cluster of marble-sized fruitlets at the tip of the panicle. These fruitlets are dark green, more curved in shape than normal developing fruit, cease growing after reaching marble size, and remain retained on the panicle for a considerable period without further growth.
The disorder is caused by a lack of pollination and fertilization resulting from aberrant weather conditions and heavy pesticide spraying that kills pollinators.
Application of NAA at 300 ppm in November on cultivar Dashehari reduces clustered panicles. Lower concentrations of NAA at 100-200 ppm also reduce clustered panicles.

Soft nose is a physiological breakdown of the flesh on the ventral side and towards the apex of mango fruits occurring while still on the tree prior to harvest. It is observed in Dashehari, Kent, and Haden cultivars. The condition known in Malaysia as 'Yeasty fruit rot' or 'Insidious fruit rot' is likely identical to soft nose.
Investigation revealed that soft nose disorder is of a physiological nature, but its cure is not known.

Jelly seed is characterised by loosening of pulp tissues and jelly formation around the stone during the advance stage of maturity of the fruit, rendering it unfit for consumption and reducing nutritional level and consumer acceptance.
Small fruit and fruit harvested when ripe, as opposed to unripe but mature, appear more prone to breakdown. Nutrient imbalance, particularly the deficiency of calcium, may be an important factor.

In India, jelly seed is restricted to cultivar Dashehari, but cultivars Chausa and Amrapali develop it when harvested late in the season. Fibrous type polyembryonic cultivar Turpentine has never exhibited such symptoms.
Preharvest spray of dihydrated calcium was found effective to reduce the occurrence of jelly seed formation.

In spongy tissue disorder, external symptoms are not visible at harvesting, but when cut in half, the flesh is pale yellow in colour, soft or spongy with or without air cavity, and has an off flavour, rendering the fruit unfit for consumption and export.

Alphonso is severely affected by spongy tissue. While earlier confined to cultivars grown in coastal regions, cultivar Mallika grown in the dry tract of the subtropical region and Dashehari from Lucknow were also found affected. In Dashehari, the disorder invariably starts from the surface of the stone, with maximum damage in the lower part compared to the middle and upper parts.
Convective heat arising from soil and intense solar radiation are reported to be the main causes for spongy tissue disorder.
Different types of mulching were found effective for the control of spongy tissue.

disease: Anthracnose, Bacterial canker, Powdery mildew, Malformation
content: Mango is mostly affected by Anthracnose, Bacterial canker, Powdery mildew, and Malformation, which cause severe loss to the crop every year.

content: The pathogen survives in soil and infected debris in the orchard.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Diseased leaves, flowers, and twigs along with fruits lying in the orchard should be collected, destroyed, pruned, and burnt to reduce inoculum levels for the next season.

content: Spray carbendazim at 0.1% twice at a 15-day interval during flowering to control blossom infection.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Spray with copper fungicides at a rate of 0.3% to effectively control foliar infection.

content: Bacterial Canker is caused by the bacterial pathogen Xanthomonas campestris pv. mangaiferaeindica.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Symptoms appear mostly on leaves as brown spots surrounded by yellow halos, usually limited by veins in the margins. The pathogen can also infect fruits, resulting in exudations from infected regions.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: The pathogen is an epiphyte and survives on mango buds and immature fruits.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Cultural preventive practices include regular inspection of orchards, adopting sanitation measures, and seedling certification to prevent pathogen establishment in new orchards.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Apply at least three sprays of streptocyclin or Agrimycin at 10-day intervals after the first visual symptom appears. Monthly sprays of carbendazim or copper oxychloride, as well as copper-based fungicides in large orchards, are also effective.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Powdery Mildew is caused by Oidium mangiferae.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Characterized by whitish powdery-like growth/mass on the leaf surface. The whole plant gets affected, including young buds, foliage, blossom, and fruits.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: The pathogen is mostly airborne and arrives in orchards from already established disease in other mango plants.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Prune diseased leaves immediately when disease appears on a few leaves, and prune malformed panicles which serve as primary sources of inoculum.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Alternate spraying of wettable sulfur at 0.2%, Tridemorph at 0.1%, and Carbendazim at 0.1% at 15-day intervals, with the first spray applied at the panicle emergence stage.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Apply three sprays of systemic fungicides during the flowering season at 12 to 15-day intervals, with the first spray applied when 25% of the flowers are open.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Mango Malformation is caused by multiple factors, with the fungal agent Fusarium mangiferae found associated with the disease.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Panicles become shortened, leaves become very small, and newly developed stems are malformed. The whole plant can be malformed if affected at an early stage.

content: The pathogen Fusarium mangiferae comes through infected seedlings and can survive in the soil.
document_name: 1  Mango diseases and their management – Integrated Disease Management

content: Avoid using scion sticks from trees bearing malformed inflorescence for propagation, and use certified saplings for propagation to prevent malformed seedlings in the orchard.

content: As soon as disease symptoms are well expressed, prune affected terminals along with approximately 15 to 20 cm of the healthy portion to eliminate the inoculum.
